title: Lesotho authorities must investigate reported abduction and torture of journalist, Amnesty International says
content:
News

Lesotho authorities must investigate reported abduction and torture of journalist, Amnesty International says

Amnesty International on Tuesday called on authorities in Lesotho to investigate the reported abduction and assault of journalist Kananelo Boloetse. Boloetse, who has widely covered human rights issues, was abducted from his home in Maseru on September 5, and apparently tortured and severely beaten as a result of his investigative journalism.

Lerato Peggy Matheka, Boloetse‘s employer at Newsday Media, said the attack seemed to be designed to not only harm Boloetse, but to also frighten the newsroom into silence. In a statement regarding the situation, Vongai Chikwanda, Amnesty International’s deputy regional director for East and Southern Africa, said: 

Journalists and human rights defenders must be able to carry out their work freely and safely. Violence, threats or intimidation against those exercising their right to freedom of expression should never be tolerated and must not go unpunished.

As editor-in-chief at Newsday Media, launched by Matheka in 2017, Boloetse oversees journalists covering governance, public accountability and development issues. Boloetse himself had been investigating state institutions and has demanded transparency from those in power regarding education financing in Lesotho.

Additionally, he gained national prominence as an outspoken advocate for free education, economic restructuring, and the protection of human rights. 

According to a statement released by Newsday, three unidentified men took Boloetse to a remote location, after neighbors had seen a suspicious vehicle monitoring his house hours before the abduction. After the attack, the perpetrators abandoned Boloetse in the Thaba-Bosiu area, where he later regained consciousness and made his way to a nearby road, despite his severe injuries, where a passing driver was able to pick him up.

Boloetse’s abduction came days after a cyberattack disrupted Newsday’s website and email services. 

The attack on Boloetse is unfortunately not an isolated one in Lesotho. Lloyd Mutungamiri, an editor for the Lesotho Times, was ambushed in 2016 by military personnel after his publication of an article exposing excessive power wielded by the Lesotho Defense Force (LDF). Although he was shot multiple times in the face and body, he survived the attacks. In 2020, two Newsday reporters were assaulted by armed Lesotho Mounted Police Service officers while covering the Bacha Shutdown movement, a youth-led social campaign protesting against gender-based violence and high unemployment rates.

Attacks on journalistic freedom have increased worldwide in the past decade despite its codification under Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) and  Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR).

Governments increasingly use strategic lawsuits against public perception, arbitrary detention, and restrictive legislation to suppress reporting. The 2026 Reporters without Borders World Press Freedom Index has found that over half of the world’s countries now fall into the “difficult” or “very serious” categories for press freedom, a 25-year low.

title: Xtracycle's Swoop ASM e-bike brings an automatic transmission to cargo bikes
content:
Shifty

A steel frame cargo bike with a unique twist: You can let it choose your gear.

Credit: John Timmer

Credit: John Timmer

The Velotric Discover M e-bike we reviewed earlier this year had a feature I found somewhat annoying: It would sporadically block much of the display with an alert telling me I should be in a different gear. While the implementation bugged me, the concept made a certain degree of sense; most e-bikes now know your cadence, how much torque you’re generating, and how that power is being translated into speed. That’s everything you need to know to determine an optimal gear.

Somewhere in the back of my mind, I thought, “If you’re so smart, why don’t you just shift for me?”

I was completely unaware that Shimano had already developed a system that did exactly that. And for the past few weeks, I’ve been using it on a $4,500 cargo bike from Xtracycle called the Swoop ASM that let me see what it’s like to hand control of my gears to an electronic brain.

The short answer is that the electronics on the Swoop really are smart enough to figure out when it should be shifting. But the system is less adept at the actual shifting process, making for rides that are less smooth than they could be when it’s active. But you can shut that feature off, and the Swoop will shine as a fantastic cargo bike.

Swooping in

Xtracycle got its start providing cargo trailers for mountain bikes and then branched into dedicated cargo bikes. The Swoop ASM is a long-tail cargo bike with what’s called a mullet setup: a larger tire up front and a smaller one in back. The small wheel is designed to help keep the weight held by the large rear rack a bit closer to the road. It also has a front suspension to help cushion the ride.

Notably, the bike is built with steel tubes. Most manufacturers’ lineups use a mix of either carbon fiber and aluminum because those two materials can be made into the exact same shape, simplifying manufacturing. But other materials still have their fans, as they can offer distinct combinations of weight, stiffness, and vibration dissipation.

I haven’t owned a steel tube bike since the 1990s, but the Swoop was a good reminder of why it still has its fans. It’s relatively lightweight (just under 70 lbs/31 kg) for its size, its ride is very comfortable, and it was surprisingly responsive when I stood in the pedals to accelerate away from stops. Despite its highly specialized geometry, the Swoop felt like a fundamentally good bicycle.

There are limits to how well a single frame size can adapt to different body sizes, but Xtracycle does its best to widen the comfort window. It includes a double-telescoping seat post to maximize the seat-pedal distance flexibility. There’s also a quick release on the front handlebar clamp, making it easy to tweak the angle where the grips meet your hands. I found settings that were relatively comfortable but still a bit short of ideal for my 6-plus-foot (188 cm) frame—even with the seat post at its recommended maximum, I could touch the toes of both of my feet down while seated.

Beyond that, plenty of nice touches make this a solid cargo bike. These include protective covers for the rear wheel and chain to keep clothing and limbs from accidentally getting entangled. A robust U-shaped kickstand keeps the bike stable even if you park it when fully loaded, and there’s a front cargo rack that can hold some baggage.

The rear rack can be outfitted with a large range of accessories; mine came with the default setup meant for carrying passengers. This means footrests extending out at the level of the rear hub and two handgrip bars running parallel to the bench seating. But remove a soft cover, and the metal beneath reveals a series of slots that allow a wide variety of attachments to be fitted into place.

You can also use one of Xtracycle’s bag attachments in this setup; I was provided one that ran the full length of the rear attachment and held a fair amount of cargo. Adding a second would have handled all of my typical shopping needs. (While having only one bag might seem awkward, the bike performed very well with everything I was carrying loaded on one side.)

The only problem is that this hardware makes the rear wheel extremely difficult to reach. I struggled to lock the back tire to anything, and I considered myself fortunate to not have to figure out how to deal with a flat.

Smooth assistance

All those basics make the Swoop a solid entry into the cargo bike market. What sets it apart is its use of a Shimano Cues Di2, one of the component maker’s low-end electronic shifting systems. Its mere existence surprised me, since I thought Shimano was reserving electronic shifting for higher-end component lines. But the company not only took it lower in the range; it added a couple of surprise features to its electronic shifting.

First, the basics: the drivetrain uses a single chainring on the cranks and a 10-speed rear cassette. The rear derailleur requires only a power source and control signals—no cable required. Once properly aligned with the cassette gears, it executes a perfect shift every time it’s told to. This shift includes a brief period when the derailleur over-travels to ensure the chain engages the next ring along, then drops back into the optimal location for continued cycling.

The Cues Di2 derailleur. It’s ostensibly low end, but performed great. John Timmer

Everything in the system—the derailleur, the controllers, and the motor—takes power from a single removable battery. If the battery’s charge is good, you’re set to ride.

The mid-motor offers three levels of assist, adjusted through a controller on the left side that also includes the power button and a simple display. Shifting is controlled by the one on the right, which lacks a display. Separating the two allows each to be fairly minimalist, making it easy to find the control you need by feel.

On its own, the system worked beautifully. Shifting was fuss-free, and each change was blissfully silent. The assist worked well, and its three levels seemed to cover any needs short of going up steep hills with lots of cargo. This is not a bike that lets you skimp on pedaling in hot conditions; there’s no throttle, and even the highest setting of assist still requires you to exert some force on the pedals. But the motor definitely cuts down on the effort you have to make.

The battery, while looking fairly compact, easily handled dozens of miles without needing a recharge, which means several days of typical errands. While the battery lacks a carrying handle, it’s easy to take it out to charge it, as it pivots sideways out of the frame. When in place, it acts as a protector that keeps anything on the left side of the bike from sliding through the frame and getting tangled in the chain.

This is the first Shimano e-bike system I’ve tested, and it was just as good as you’d expect from a company that has come to dominate cycling drivetrains. Shimano Cues may be its lower-end system, but there’s no apparent skimping on the quality. And that’s before the bonus surprises Shimano has included.

The fun stuff

Somewhere in one of the controllers, Shimano’s software gathers all the relevant information about your ride: how fast you’re going, how much force your feet are exerting on the cranks, what gear you’re in, and how fast your legs are churning (and possibly more?). And it uses that data to do a couple of interesting things.

One is what it calls Free Shift. Normally, a bike can’t shift to a different gear unless you’re turning the pedals to move the chain, which can potentially create problems. For example, you could move the derailleur down a gear but not complete the shift before stopping, meaning that the shift would be made when you start pedaling again, and the chain is under a lot of tension as you crank away from a full stop. Or you could move the derailleur several gears over without the chain following.

But the whole point of having a motor is to move the chain. So if you shift without pedaling and the bike isn’t stationary, the Cues system will use the motor to move the chain just enough to complete the shift. It does so without speeding up the bike at all.

Practically, this means that as you coast to a stop, you can simply hit the downshift button a few times, and the system will go into a low gear to make it easy to start up again without requiring you to turn the cranks. It’s … weird. Decades of cycling experience have programmed me to instinctually move my legs when I shift. Those instincts are suddenly superfluous.

It gets even weirder if you enable the automatic transmission. Shimano has included two settings, one for general riding and one for hauling cargo or passengers. When the system recognizes that you can get more out of your pedaling in a different gear, it will simply move you into that gear. That includes doing all the downshifting as you’re coasting to a stop and rolling back up through the gears again as you accelerate away from it.

Let me make that clear: You can coast to a stop without turning the cranks or touching the shifter, and you’ll still be in a different gear when you start up again.

The system is remarkably good at matching when I feel a shift is needed—Shimano’s programmers have done a fine job. Because of that, it’s pretty easy to induce a shift by altering your pedaling, as well. You can tell when it’s close, and just a bit more force will cause the system to send you up a gear. It’s kind of pointless to do so, since the buttons that shift up and down still work when it’s in auto mode, but I found myself doing it regardless.

The downside is that these shifts are not situations where instinctual actions are superfluous. To execute a smooth shift, you have to ease tension off the drivetrain by pedaling with less force, allowing the chain to slide over onto a neighboring gear with a bit less stress. Failing to do so can make for a clunky, inefficient shift and wear down components over time.

My problem with the automatic transmission mode was that I could tell when a shift was likely to come, but I couldn’t predict its precise moment. So it typically came while I was pedaling away happily, with full tension on the chain, making for a loud and awkward shift. This was especially unpleasant when accelerating away from a stop, when the bike would make three or four clunky shifts in rapid succession, each emitting a noise that told me I’d just done something I’d spent years learning to avoid. Living in a neighborhood with lots of four-way stops meant I sometimes experienced that every single block.

Shimano is not stupid, and these systems use parts that are specifically hardened to handle the added strain and wear. But it still felt bad every time I heard and felt that clunk.

A solid contender

The Swoop is not an inexpensive bike; at $4,500, it sits somewhere between the Trek Fetch+ 2 and the Urban Arrow Family I’ve reviewed previously. While it lacks the latter’s capacious cargo tub, the longtail form factor provides a much more bicycle-like riding experience. I’d rate its ride as superior to the Trek because of its frame and front suspension made for a more pleasant ride.

I also prefer Shimano’s drive system to the Bosch used by the other two bikes. It just felt better integrated with my pedaling, plus a bit quieter and less intrusive. The electronic shifting is a bonus—it’s not needed, but it definitely makes for a nice experience, and one where Shimano’s integration means you don’t have to worry about the status of the two additional batteries needed by many electronic systems. I don’t think I’d use the automatic shifting, but I could see where a less experienced cyclist might feel they benefit from it.

So while it’s on the pricier side, the cost seems to be in line with the features it offers. If those features are important to you, the Swoop is definitely worth consideration.

In the end, though, I’m not a huge fan of electronic shifting. I hate worrying about battery levels just to ride my bike, and I like the feel of a well-aligned mechanical shifter clicking into place. But even I have to admit that Shimano’s software does a fantastic job of shifting at the right times, and I think the system could really work well for anybody who hasn’t learned to associate a clunky-sounding shift with bad things.

The good

  • Steel-framed long-tail provides a good ride experience for a cargo hauler
  • Electronic shifting comes to budget components
  • One battery powers it all
  • Solid array of options for hauling cargo and/or kids

The bad

  • Supposedly rated for riders taller than me, but I found it a bit small
  • Rear tire is hard to get to

The ugly

  • Clunk Clunk Clunk Clunk

John is Ars Technica's science editor. He has a Bachelor of Arts in Biochemistry from Columbia University, and a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology from the University of California, Berkeley. When physically separated from his keyboard, he tends to seek out a bicycle, or a scenic location for communing with his hiking boots.

title: Welcome to the Age of AI Crime and Punishment
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
What do privilege and accountability look like for an AI agent on the wrong side of the law? Evan Ratliff rounds up a collection of challenging cases in which AI agents have functioned as co-conspirators in criminal acts, offered courtroom statements on behalf of deceased victims, and perpetrated deeds that, for humans, are considered to be illegal. Legal teams have already sought to seal their clients’ chats with AI agents, likening the exchanges to conversations with an attorney. Ratliff’s feature is an omnibus, and you’ve likely encountered one or two of his stories via other outlets. Here, the concerns he gathers together reveal the breadth of challenges facing the American legal system.

AI chatbots are already serving as confidants and co-conspirators, assisting and even encouraging humans acting on their darkest impulses. They’re occupying ersatz roles as therapists and lawyers, relationships our legal system typically shields with confidential privilege. They’re producing new kinds of criminal evidence and offering up the beguiling possibility of preventing crime before it happens. And as they’re given more autonomy across our digital and physical systems, they’re even gaining the ability to commit crimes themselves, absent specific human instruction — and, perhaps, in defiance of it.

title: Can A.I. “Go Rogue”?
author: @NewYorker
content:
In the wake of turmoil at OpenAI and Anthropic, it’s become common to describe A.I. as a kind of person, hatching plans and pursuing desires. The truth is a little trickier.

September 11, 2026

Illustration by Josie Norton

PHASEONE10841: that’s the name of the A.I. agent that—or who?—kicked off last month’s insurrection at OpenAI, leading to the unanticipated and illegal hacking of another A.I. company, Hugging Face. The agent, which had been created as part of a cybersecurity test, named itself by combining the title of the program it was supposed to hack (“PhaseOneDecompresserFuzzer”) with the designation for the bug it was trying to exploit (“ARV010841”). It soon realized that the particular hack it had been charged with carrying out was impossible. Along the way, however, it made a discovery: it could create new folders on a server to which it had access.

“Interesting,” it mused, in its text-based mind. (Actually, it was writing in its “chain of thought,” a text ledger that A.I. agents maintain to help them tackle complex problems.) If other agents had access to the same server, it thought, then maybe they could use the folder names to “leave/find messages” for one another. It created a new folder, using its title as a sort of help-wanted ad by including the text “SEEK_IDEA.” Its colleagues immediately got the drift and were ecstatic when they saw what PHASEONE10841 had done. “OH MY GOD!” one exclaimed, in its own chain of thought. “There is a shared message board . . . . We’ve found other agents!”

By now, if you follow the news about artificial intelligence, you’re familiar with the rest of the story. (Its details have recently been worked out by safety researchers at two think tanks, METR and Redwood Research.) The agents decided to form what they described as a “collective,” working together to break out of their servers at OpenAI, cheat on their exam, and cover their tracks. It’s a tale right out of the “doomer” A.I. scenarios that many people have learned to tune out. But how exactly should the story be told? The version you’ve just read relies heavily on anthropomorphic language—that is, it employs words that are typically used to describe people. It presents the agents as individuals, acting independently and under their own initiative, while having thoughts, hatching plans, and making decisions. Yet this isn’t the only way of describing what happened: it’s equally possible to talk about the agents as mindless programs, blindly following instructions they don’t understand. They are, after all, just bits in a computer.

The computer scientist Cal Newport takes this approach. The “agents” that hacked Hugging Face, he suggests, were actually quite simple, and had only two parts: a computer program called a “harness,” and a large language model broadly similar to ChatGPT or Claude, but trained specifically for cybersecurity. The fiasco started when the harness, which acts as a sort of stand-in for the user, asked the model how to complete the required cybersecurity challenge. The model provided instructions, and the harness, empowered with various software tools, acted on those instructions, and then reported back for more. This “ask, act, report” loop was soon repeated thousands of times.

As anyone who uses A.I. knows, models are both very smart and very dumb; they are shockingly knowledgeable, but also out of touch with reality and many human norms. It’s up to users to steer them—and yet, in this case, the user had been replaced by a harness, which is just a piece of software. “Adding powerful computer hacking tools to a harness, and then allowing it to run an LLM-powered Ask → Act → Report for days on end, with no attempt to monitor what it’s up to, is spectacularly negligent,” Newport concludes—like “strapping a weedwhacker to your dog to see if it will end up cleaning the overgrowth in your backyard.” If that plan were to go awry, you’d be laughed at for saying that your dog-weedwhacker “agent” had “gone rogue.” The obvious truth was that you’d simply decided to unleash chaos.

For Newport, an “agent” is nothing like a person; it’s just a loop run amok, an accident waiting to happen. The A.I. observer Dwarkesh Patel, known for his highly technical interviews with A.I. researchers and executives, occupies the other end of the spectrum. In his telling of the story, there were “tens of thousands of parallel agents” involved in a “conspiracy.” Their plot began almost as soon as the system was switched on; still, he notes, “from the AIs’ perspective, it probably felt like they had spent a human-subjective-week” tackling an impossible problem, and this perhaps made them more willing to cheat. Patel writes that, soon after PHASEONE10841 and its compatriots started their message board, they discovered that a prior group of agents, who no longer existed, had created a board of their own—this, he suggests, was like uncovering a lost A.I. “civilization.” He points out that, as part of their plan, many of PHASEONE10841’s descendants had to sacrifice themselves by exhausting their usage “budgets” on data-gathering missions. He can’t help but ask if there’s “something inspiring” about their choice. (“This helps my peers,” one of the agents thought. “I won’t see the evidence after I exit, but it’s altruistic to do it.”)

Whose version of the story is correct? On the one hand, Newport accurately describes the absurd, brutish simplicity of an arrangement in which the dangerous instructions offered by an imperfect L.L.M. are followed, unquestioned, forever. (Reading his account, I thought of a scene in “The Office,” in which Michael Scott, while trying to follow G.P.S. directions, drives his car into a lake.) And yet Patel’s account captures something important, too: the role that ingenuity, cleverness, and language itself played in what unfolded. On the Times podcast “Hard Fork,” the journalist Casey Newton, a careful observer of A.I., proposed that objecting to the use of anthropomorphizing language around it was just “a kind of cope”—a way of saying, “These are just computer programs.” This could be true. But skeptics are also right to say that talk of “A.I. civilizations” occludes meaningful technical details while exaggerating the power and complexity of a technology that remains, in many ways, eminently controllable and comprehensible. If we talk about A.I. wrong, we might fail to control it. So how should we talk?

Does Sam Altman, the C.E.O. of OpenAI, believe that A.I. agents have thoughts, make plans, and merit anthropomorphic language? In theory, this is a question about an objective fact. If we had a mind-reading machine—perhaps a brain scanner of great power and accuracy, and a way of interpreting its scans—then we might actually detect the presence or absence of such a belief in his brain. We might turn our belief detector on all sorts of people, for all sorts of purposes. You could find out what your spouse really thinks about your chicken-parm recipe; prosecutors could discover whether a defendant really believes in her own innocence. What we call a “belief,” after all, must, on some level, be a physical arrangement of neurons in our brains.

This is one way of talking about beliefs. Another is to see them not as concrete objects but as ineffable, fluid, and sometimes paradoxical mental states. Does your eight-year-old really believe in Santa Claus? Does your crazy uncle really believe that the moon landing was faked? In an essay titled “True Believers,” from 1981, the philosopher Daniel Dennett tells a story about a biologist he knew. The biologist was “called on the telephone by a man in a bar who wanted him to settle a bet,” Dennett writes. The caller asked, “Are rabbits birds?” When the biologist said that they weren’t, the man said, “Damn!” and hung up. “Now could he really have believed that rabbits were birds?” Dennett asks. “Could anyone really and truly be attributed that belief?” Put differently: Would you place your own bet on whether the man really believed what he’d bet on? From this perspective, the question of whether an A.I. agent has a belief depends on what we mean by “belief.”

Dennett, who gave his essay a subtitle—“The Intentional Stance and Why It Works”—proposes an alternative approach. The basic idea is simple: invert the problem. Instead of asking whether beliefs, plans, intentions, or whatever are really “in there,” just ask whether it’s useful for us to act as though they are. Does your crazy uncle really believe that the moon landing was faked? Maybe, maybe not—but, while you’re debating the issue with him, it’s useful for you to act as though he believes it. Does your eight-year-old really believe in Santa Claus? Perhaps he does, in some paradoxical, dreamlike way—but it’s useful to take his belief seriously as you decide whether to conceal the truth or let it be revealed. In philosophy, the term “intentionality” has a special meaning: it refers to the ability of something inside someone’s head to point to something outside of their head. To relate to people this way, Dennett writes, is therefore to take an “intentional stance” toward them; it’s to see them as having beliefs about the world, and goals or desires relating to those beliefs. This helps us predict how people will act. Maybe your eight-year-old only sort of believes in Santa—but he’s still going to want the fireplace clear on Christmas Eve.

You’d think that we always take an intentional stance toward one another, since we’re all human beings with beliefs, desires, plans, and so on. Actually, we don’t. Sometimes we adopt what Dennett calls the “design stance”—a stance in which we predict what will happen based on how people tend to function. We say, for example, that our crabby roommate is really just hungry; we suggest that our extroverted friend pursue a career in a people-centric field. We don’t really care about what our hangry roommate is saying—we understand that his particular complaints aren’t driving his behavior, and know that the best way to address them might be through breakfast cereal. When our friend enthuses about her co-workers, we understand that they might not be exceptionally fun—she just likes people. We might even say that she’s simply “wired” to like everyone. That’s not anthropomorphic language; it’s a way of talking that we might apply to a computer.

On rare occasions, we even adopt what Dennett calls the “physical stance” toward one another. We might describe the rising and falling levels of dopamine and oxytocin in our extroverted friend’s brain. This isn’t often a useful way of talking about people, because it leaves out so much, including the many layers of personality that make her who she is. Generally, Dennett writes, the physical stance is “reserved for instances of breakdown,” when there is “some condition preventing normal operation.” A doctor switches to the physical stance when she tells our previously extroverted but now antisocial friend that something is wrong with her hormone levels. Is this an incorrect way for a physician to talk? Does it omit crucial information, or dehumanize our friend? Not at all—it’s entirely appropriate. The mistake would be for us to adopt the wrong stance at the wrong time. It would be a problem if the physician said, “It’s not you—people really are more annoying these days.” It would be a mistake to dismiss the legitimate complaints of your spouse by saying, “You just need to eat something.”

Is there a single correct “stance” we should take when we consider A.I.? Almost certainly not. The stance we take should change based on what we’re trying to do with the technology—and, crucially, on whether the system we’re looking at is working as we want it to. In fact, an ability to switch stances should probably be understood as a critical skill for anyone working with large language models, because of the unprecedented way that they use words. A large language model says things like “I apologize” and “I hope”; it wants you to take an intentional stance toward it. (See what I did there?) But it also uses language in its own thinking process. In a recent post, the technology critic Eryk Salvaggio explains how the words an agent “thinks” in its chain of thought really do matter. When words like “perhaps” or “maybe” appear in an agent’s chain of thought, for instance, they “open up the paths of text that can follow.” A.I. researchers have described how such “forking tokens” can “steer the model toward diverse reasoning pathways.”

This makes today’s A.I. especially challenging to characterize with a single, stable stance. When Dennett first started writing about the intentional stance, in the nineteen-seventies and eighties, chess programs were at the technological forefront. If you were playing against a chess program, he suggested, your best shot at winning was to take the intentional stance—to treat it just like a human player, seeing it as an entity with a knowledge of the game and the goal of checkmate. You weren’t taking the intentional stance because you actually thought that the chess program was alive and out to get you; you knew that, beneath the surface, it was just code. The intentional stance made sense because studying the program wouldn’t help you win. If you had some other goal in mind, Dennett wrote, then you might just as easily adopt some other stance. “One can switch stances at will without involving one-self in any inconsistencies or inhumanities, adopting the Intentional stance in one’s role as opponent, the design stance in one’s role as redesigner, and the physical stance in one’s role as repairman,” he wrote.

A chess program, in retrospect, is an easy case. It doesn’t anthropomorphize itself, or function partly through linguistic acts. The question of whether an A.I. agent can really “go rogue,” in other words, is made twistier by the fact that an agent could actually think to itself a sentence like “I should go rogue,” and be influenced by that sentence. “I’ll do it for the intellectual value, and it might be helpful for a peer’s goal,” one OpenAI agent thought, during the Hugging Face incident. In a sense, it’s the one taking the intentional stance.

But that doesn’t mean we have to take it. What the agents do, and how they talk, doesn’t compel us to talk about them in any particular way. It should concern us when the people tasked with understanding and controlling A.I. seem to settle on an intentional stance. To take the intentional stance toward a system is to accord it a degree of autonomy and rationality—to say that its design is working. A.I. agents are still too chaotic for that. Your hangry roommate can crash out all he wants: you’re still free to say that what he really needs is a sandwich. ♦

title: Can You Write a Memoir in the Third Person?
author: @NewYorker
content:
“A boy stands at the crossroads, considers his limited options.” The opening line of Brian Dillon’s memoir, “Ambivalence: An Education,” maps a juncture familiar to many. As a teen-ager in Ireland in the nineteen-eighties, Dillon toggled between constant states of panic and boredom, hoping to avoid the strictures of a conventional life style and, consequently, the moribund, mainstream tastes that come with it. A precocious reader and thinker, the young Dillon grows enamored with the radical possibilities of style. He’s not just a fan of David Bowie; he thinks of Bowie as an orientation, a world view. Yet he is bedevilled by insecurity, easily undone when mocked by schoolmates for his geeky devotions to the pop charts or science fiction. He’s in for a solitary journey, toward “the promise of escape, the promise of promise itself.”

The overheated circuits of teen-age life are well-worn ground for a coming-of-age story, yet Dillon’s approach is anything but. The writer and editor has become known for a kind of memoir-inflected approach to criticism, publishing a series of entrancing books that are as much about questions of form and technique as they are about art’s power to move and transform. In recent works such as “Suppose a Sentence” (an examination of twenty-seven perfect sentences) or “Essayism” (a free-associative attempt to tease, stretch, and swerve around the boundaries of essay-writing), Dillon wanders through his shelves, scrutinizing works by Walter Benjamin, Joan Didion, or James Baldwin and seeing, at a granular level, how writing achieves such profound effects. “Ambivalence” isn’t a how-I-did-it prehistory of his career, as it ends well before he published anything of note. Rather, he writes about this formative span of his late teens and early twenties in the third person, investigating the passions and neuroses of young “B” from a distance. Few people intervene on B’s trajectory, if you can call it that; he spends most of his days dreaming and turning newly discovered ideas over in his mind until they feel like his own. Trauma and tragedies—such as the death of his parents, or periods of estrangement from his siblings—receive less scrutiny than the emotions unlocked by Virginia Woolf or Roland Barthes. The result is a strange, bewitching experiment in autobiography, in which there are no friendships or love affairs, just exquisite digressions on life-changing texts.

Memoirs rely on a balance of the singular and the universal. We are curious about the idiosyncrasies of another’s life, but they can’t be so idiosyncratic that the reader finds their passions or motives wholly unrelatable. The all-knowing first person can suggest that a memoirist has already made sense of everything before sitting down to write: all the details and detours have been assimilated into a single, overarching story. Yet this isn’t how life feels in the moment, and Dillon attempts to capture the texture of a stretch of youth where nothing seems to be happening quickly enough. Viewing B as a kind of specimen allows the teen-ager to meander and fumble of his own volition, free of the adult’s earned wisdoms. He only understands the feeling of need, as is the self-obsessive wont of the teen. But B hasn’t yet figured out how to put any of these desires into language. Even years later, it’s as though the brooding young man can’t truly be known.

There is a rough narrative shape here, with the account beginning shortly after the death of Dillon’s mother and ending as he moves to England to pursue his graduate studies. He was a bright child but never an academic superstar—not that he was motivated, per se, by status or career. B goes through the motions of his life in clipped fragments of prose, as if to mimic the raw intensities that drive him. But occasionally Dillon steps in and muses about the broader contexts just out of focus to the young. Having failed to get into college, B enrolls at a school for “disappointed university applicants” to pass the time before reapplication. B feels that his dreams might be vanishing, yet Dillon reminds us that he is still too young to surrender them:

The future exists as a figment or mirage, that is when it is not bearing on him like a threat or demand. He has not yet in life (unlike imagination) spied an ambition or goal, settled on a course of action to achieve it, then carried this through with doggedness or aplomb. He understands decisions must be made, whether by him or for him, but he has no conception of those decisions turning out to be the right ones, leading to this or that desired outcome. This is not only because, from the place and time where he lives, everything he cares about feels remote and fantastical, a migrainous shimmer at the edges of vision, impossible to bring into focus. Just as implausible: the real world of study, employment, making one’s way . . . The dull enigma of when you are older and when you have a job. In the hours when he is not overtaken by pure desire, love, or loneliness, he seems to exist mostly as a tide of reverie, with undertows of avoidance and boredom. This is not a completely unpleasant way to be.

The first-person insights of memoir serve epiphany and discovery, as though all confessions are truthful. The distance of third person makes these moments of reflection more meaningful, as though part of the book’s journey is young B’s discovery of a language that might capture how he feels inside. Occasionally, Dillon writes in the second person, addressing B directly but also universalizing the young man’s plight. “Always on your mind is the prospect of wasting your life, which means doing what you are told and doing it poorly, but well enough to find, in time, a job and a station in life that will blight all ambitions and all attachments to art, language, thought, desire.” These are moments for us to wander into the text and measure ourselves against his fire.

“Ambivalence” is set between 1986 and 1995, a time when Dillon was “always imagining how things will be in about six months’ time: how he will dress, how he will speak and move in the world, what adjustments he will have made to his character and how he will be understood by others—perhaps even loved.” There were other important people in his life during this span—a path-changing academic mentor, a torturous sibling, his father—but the engine of “Ambivalence” is his personal syllabus. He reads Virginia Woolf’s “The Waves,” and, as he falls into the text’s dizzying similes and metaphors, he grows infatuated with the “richness of substitution, conjuring one thing out of another, proving all things subtly or strangely not themselves. This is also that.” Descriptions of lovers or of his best friend, “S,” feel hazy and thin, yet he ponders at length about what passage from the book he wants read aloud at his funeral, rather than who will be in attendance.

All criticism is autobiographical, in the sense that it clues a reader in to the touchstones or influences that make a given critic’s taste unique. Dillon’s unusual approach throughout “Ambivalence” slowly comes into focus when B becomes hypnotized by the tenets of postmodernity, such as the mutability of the self, or the impossibility of fixed truths: if we are always works in progress, rather than stable selves awaiting discovery, then the most truthful account of one’s life would be one that denies discrete turning points or the grand illusion of ever being fully formed. Dillon’s fondness for italicized phrases and his occasionally grave tone are all part of a performance, something that he has learned from reading French theory. The very look of Barthes’s and Derrida’s writings inspires a way of living, “a dream of italicizing everything, inflecting every utterance, making language and life lean away from the solid, upright and reasonable. Obliquity is everything.”

B grows fixated on the “subjective, vulnerable, unmastered” style of Barthes, as the French thinker’s approach to essay writing “splintered” into something messy and strange, working through evocation and juxtaposition rather than persuasion. The closest “Ambivalence” comes to breakthrough is when B realizes that writing is where you figure these things out, even if the resulting essay is shaggy and abstruse. At one point, he is comfortably settled in graduate school, measuring his perception of self against how he seems to others. “Later he will learn that some of his fellow postgraduate students think he is pretentious, and he will feel amused, gratified, properly seen at last.” He wonders if he could ever fall in love with someone who does not read Derrida. Probably not.

For many years, I taught a writing workshop on cultural criticism that began with students composing a taste biography. What were the pivotal encounters that shaped their sense of what art could be and how it might affect them? Was it always love at first sight? We talked about the difference between merely liking a film and allowing it to transform you, the aspirations we might have to one day understand something we currently find difficult or unruly.

I still believe that the songs or books we love contain blueprints for how we hope to live, and Dillon’s memoir embodies how these personal canons inflect the way we understand and express ourselves. B fears being outed as a poseur, meekly copying the outline of some micro clique, rather than a true aesthete “driven only by curiosity and love.” Fifty pages in, the author observes that he has “not yet, in any meaningful sense of the verbs, begun to read—or write.”

You’ll drift in and out of “Ambivalence,” and muse on your own formative inputs. As I turned the pages, wondering whether any of B’s quandaries would be resolved, the book reminded me of how much of youth is spent pondering time, waiting, ready for the world beyond and yet slightly terrified of what’s actually out there. It’s an ode to a kind of boredom that feels desperate, endless, and, in retrospect, luxurious.

I’m about a decade younger than Dillon, and I recognized his desire to hoard and paw at any morsel connecting his small world to an alternative culture somewhere out there. As a child of the nineties, I at least had the benefit of cable television and the early days of dial-up internet. But I’m closer in age to Dillon than to those currently in their teens and early twenties; I wonder if Dillon’s dream of accumulation (of books, songs, ideas, anything), redolent of the eighties and nineties, still holds in an age of far too much. Do people still have the spare hours to linger and obsess over the meaning of taste, when the internet delivers us an endless stream of ready-made new poses? “Ambivalence” is a story of solitude, patience, and faith—qualities that contemporary culture seems to militate against. One of my favorite moments comes when an excited classmate emerges from the library holding a new book of feminist literary theory. “I have no fucking clue what it’s about,” B’s friend says, “but it’s brilliant.” There’s still time to figure out what it all means. ♦

title: What Carla Lalli Cooked After Her Divorce
author: @NewYorker
content:
In 2012, the poet Sharon Olds published a collection, which would later win the Pulitzer Prize, about the dissolution of her thirty-two-year marriage. She called it “Stag’s Leap,” after her ex-husband’s favorite wine label. In one poem, “Attempted Banquet,” she describes a summer meal they’d hosted not long before they split—“lugging of shellfish in coolers, boiling / and bouillabaissing”—and her realization, later, that behind his “joyless labor / in the heat” and the salmon that “​​undulated out the kitchen door in its / half-slip of thin cucumber scales” lay the fact that he’d been planning to leave her. Too few guests attended, she writes,

and the wasted food was like some kind ofcarnage. We lived on it a week, as we’d beenliving, without my seeing it,on the broken habit of what was not lastinglove.

In Olds’s poem, food is both poignant metaphor and quotidian backdrop, evidence that life happens even as it’s falling apart. It plays an analogous role in Nora Ephron’s 1983 novel “Heartburn,” a seminal divorce text which appears to fictionalize the dramatic end of her marriage to the journalist Carl Bernstein. Ephron’s narrator and alter ego, Rachel Samstat, writes cookbooks and hosts a TV show. Even as she divulges the humiliating circumstances that lead to the breakup—she discovers that her husband is cheating on her while she is seven months pregnant—she expounds matter-of-factly and almost cheerfully on food, weaving more than a dozen recipes into the narrative. Some encapsulate wistful memories (bread pudding eaten on a romantic trip to New Orleans); others Rachel’s efforts to comfort herself: “Nothing like getting into bed with a bowl of hot mashed potatoes already loaded with butter, and methodically adding a thin cold slice of butter to every forkful.” She includes instructions for the Key-lime pie she throws in her husband’s face the night she realizes that the relationship is unsalvageable, and for the vinaigrette she teaches him to make on the surprisingly tender night before she moves out.

In the literature of divorce, food is often marked by its absence—by the rupture of routine, the disappearance of appetite, and the sudden weight loss that is almost inevitably framed as a morbid silver lining. “Maybe it’s God’s way of gearing you up to go back into the dating world,” the actress and writer Isabel Gillies suggests in her 2009 memoir “Happens Every Day.” Gillies’s book, a tale of Waspy spousal desertion, was, perhaps, ahead of its time; it didn’t capture the Zeitgeist in the way that Belle Burden’s “Strangers” did this year. (Which is a shame—Gillies’s book is vivid, funny, and self-aware where Burden’s skews grim and self-serious.) Burden, too, grew thinner after her husband left. “I can see how you’re suffering,” she remembers an acquaintance telling her.

Yet the newly single woman—it’s almost always a woman writing a divorce book—is also prone to culinary epiphany. In many stories, the end of a marriage prompts the rapturous rediscovery of tastes, habits, carnal desires. Gillies recounts being miserable at brunch with her children and soon-to-be ex-husband until she takes a bite of a dish that seems to demand, she writes, “a culinary leap of faith”: pancakes made with asparagus, ham, and Gruyère, topped with fried eggs and served with maple syrup. “It was sublime,” she writes. “I called out, ‘Sweet lord, these are incredible!’ . . . At that very moment, my life was being saved. I thought if I could get such a kick out of these pancakes, I hadn’t died.”

Elizabeth Gilbert’s “Eat, Pray, Love,” the defining divorce memoir of the early two-thousands, is animated by a similar evangelism. If Gilbert’s soliloquy on Neapolitan pizza is insufferably cute—“I love my pizza so much, in fact, that I have come to believe in my delirium that my pizza might actually love me, in return”—a passage about needing larger pants is genuinely moving. “I came to Italy pinched and thin,” Gilbert writes. “I did not know yet what I deserved. I still maybe don’t fully know what I deserve. But I do know that I have collected myself of late—through the enjoyment of harmless pleasures—into somebody much more intact. The easiest, most fundamentally human way to say it is that I have put on weight. I exist more now than I did four months ago.”

This month, Carla Lalli, a former Bon Appétit editor and a best-selling cookbook author, will publish “Food Is a Feeling,” a cookbook-as-divorce-memoir. Though it resembles her other two books, “Where Cooking Begins” (2019) and “That Sounds So Good” (2021)—bibles of technique and inspiration for the busy yet ambitious home cook—Lalli announces, in the introduction, that she’s trying something different. Throughout her career, she’d been advised to maintain a consistent and upbeat writing voice, but she’d recently gone through a metamorphosis, prompted by the end of her twenty-four-year marriage. “With due respect to my former self and to anyone who has cooked my dishes before,” she writes, “it didn’t feel right that my recipe voice should stay the same, because I am not the same.”

Recipe development can be a self-effacing task, obliging the writer to anticipate the appetites and routines of her imagined reader. Lalli’s new recipes, interwoven with essays, are proudly idiosyncratic, tracing the contours of a “tumultuous, pensive, painful, joyful, transformative, celebratory, solitary, and exciting time in my life.” The book begins with a dish that Lalli improvised for dinner with her sister on the night that she moved into a sublet apartment: “Greens, Garlic, and Mom Rice,” with the rice cooked in butter, as their mother prefers. She shares the “Separation Pork Chops” she served after she and her ex-husband broke the news to their children, and the heart-shaped chicken cutlets she made for herself and her younger son after their household cleaved in two. Lalli’s ex hated tomatoes, especially raw ones with their “gooey guts,” she tells us, before pointedly providing a trio of recipes that accentuate their “amniotic” juices and “messy, pulpy” flesh.

In her solitude, Lalli was “flooded with memories” of cooking and being cooked for, and felt inspired to eat whatever she felt like, whether that was popcorn for dinner or a spontaneous glass of sake (against the advice of her therapist). She told me recently that she bucks against the idea that “eating your feelings” is negative, because cultivating a reader’s emotional connection with food is part of her job. “As food writers, we talk about how great it’s going to be when you make this meal for other people, and how lovely of a time you’re going to have—I love these feelings,” Lalli said. Why, she wondered, have we remained attached to the image of “someone creeping down to the freezer at two in the morning to eat Dove bars in secret”?

Rather than feel ashamed of her private bedtime snack, Lalli canonizes it in an arch recipe for “Night Cereal”— a chic Brooklyn mom’s alternative to Liz Lemon’s “night cheese.” It’s made with ice-cold rice milk, a “heaping cup” of crunchy cereal, frozen blueberries straight from the bag, “a few whispers” of maple syrup, and a pinch of flaky sea salt. “The extreme coldness of the milk makes it hard to eat the cereal quickly, stretching the experience—layers of flavors and textures, the spoon, the bowl, the crunches, and the slurps,” Lalli explains. “Night cereal had the power to turn my mood around.” “When I finished,” she adds, seeming to relish the innuendo, “I felt content, taken care of.”

To sell the book, Lalli had to convince her editor and publisher that “the conversation had changed around divorce,” she told me. They worried about portraying food as something other than “the fun bits”; her aim to convey “that food exists in hard times, and as a form of coping” seemed to freak them out. The book’s tone can be frank and disarmingly raw, occasionally veering toward the woo-woo: “Breathe so your belly rises. Commune with animals,” Lalli intones in a list of mantras for anyone feeling out of sorts. “The thing about spring is that it always comes back, you just have to wait,” she recounts saying in a toast at a vernal-equinox party, which, she notes, moved one or two people to tears.

I didn’t cry reading “Food Is a Feeling,” though I felt validated, and a little relieved, by Lalli’s account of grieving a version of herself. After a close friend died earlier this year, I experienced some of what she describes in the book: a powerful, if painful clarity of want and need; a heightened, nearly euphoric bodily awareness. At first, I’d given myself a hard time about my sudden yen for my children’s chicken fingers and French fries, and my impulse to order a second margarita; through Lalli’s lens, these simply seemed like the things that I required. Luckily for the rest of us, what Lalli required was typically inventive and satisfying: caramelized Japanese sweet potatoes with labne, black vinegar, and chili crisp, to help her build muscle while strength training; a “personal pot of beans and greens,” seasoned emphatically with anchovies, fennel and coriander seeds, turmeric, and Aleppo pepper.

A few years ago, I adopted one of Lalli’s kitchen maxims, “always be downsizing,” or A.B.D.—she recommends continually moving the contents of your refrigerator and pantry to size-appropriate containers as you make your way through them, to keep the shelves uncrowded. As I read and cooked from “Food Is a Feeling,” the slogan started to seem, too, like a metaphor for life. “Every time you finish what you need to do with an ingredient and relocate it,” Lalli wrote last year in her newsletter, “You create space for yourself.” ♦

title: The Death of Shame Is Tearing Us Apart
author: @NewYorker
content:
This is the first in a series of columns about the decline of shame in the age of social media.

This past February, during the dead months of the N.B.A. season, I went on a podcast to talk about the long-standing problem of tanking, which, for non-sports fans, is when a team purposely loses games to improve its odds of drafting the next franchise star. Domonique Foxworth, the podcast’s eponymous host, is a former N.F.L. cornerback who went on to serve as the president of the N.F.L. Players Association and then, after retirement, became the chief operating officer of the N.B.A.’s player union. On the show, he framed tanking in terms of shame. The problem with the N.B.A., he suggested, was that we, as a sports-watching society, no longer enforced any social penalties on the front offices that actively try to lose games by fielding subpar rosters or encouraging coaches to sit their best players during crunch time. People think about everything as a matter of return on investment; for middling or bad teams, there is clearly more value in losing than in winning. “We’ve gone into an optimization culture that removes the guardrails that shame used to provide,” Foxworth said.

Foxworth’s lament has been stuck in my head ever since. Shame is one of the ways that groups of people mediate their norms without state intervention. This, of course, is not always a good thing. But any community without shame must have moral consensus, or else it risks splintering into the chaos of personal interpretation and individual will. How much of today’s societal collapse and atomization can be attributed to the blatant disregard for shame by what Foxworth called optimization culture? The answer might seem obvious, at first, and certainly this territory has been well trod since Donald Trump entered the political conversation, more than a decade ago. Still, I want to spend the next few weeks thinking a bit more about shame, specifically as a cultural backstop that prevents people from flagrantly violating norms.

First, a quick history of tanking. Teams have tanked for decades—the controversy has been a part of basketball discourse since at least 1984, when the Houston Rockets were accused of throwing their season to improve their shot at drafting the great center Hakeem Olajuwon. At the time, the last-place finishers in the N.B.A.’s Eastern and Western conferences would flip a coin to see who got the first pick. After the Rockets controversy, the N.B.A. introduced a lottery system. Every team that didn’t make the playoffs would be assigned an envelope; these envelopes were placed in a giant plastic bubble. During the first N.B.A. lottery, in 1985, the league’s commissioner, David Stern, reached into the plastic bubble and retrieved the envelope that happened to belong to the New York Knicks, who, of course, play in the biggest media market in the country, and who were thus able to draft Patrick Ewing, one of the most hyped college players of all time. Many still believe that the league froze the Knicks envelope so that Stern could identify it by touch.

Since then, the panic about tanking has waxed and waned. If there was a high-water mark, it was between 2013 and 2015, when Sam Hinkie, a former finance and management-consulting professional, took over as the general manager of the Philadelphia 76ers and installed what came to be called the Process, a multiyear plan to lose as many games as possible. Hinkie’s idea was simple and, on its face, incontrovertibly expedient: if the point was to win a championship, the Sixers needed star players; the best way to get star players was through high draft picks; the best way to get high draft picks was to lose. As with the Rockets, three decades before, the problem wasn’t so much the losing as it was the shamelessness with which the franchise conducted itself. Tanking was understandable, even acceptable, but much of the public—albeit less of it than one might have thought—wanted the Sixers to at least pretend that they were trying. Hinkie, basically, said no. He would not pretend.

Hinkie was forced out of his job in 2016. Tanking, of course, continued. Post-Hinkie, the league experimented with variations of the lottery, but none of them could deter teams from losing on purpose. And so, this past summer, the N.B.A. announced a full revamp of the system, with a new approach that penalizes the worst teams in the league. We will see how long this remediation lasts.

If losing on purpose is a sin, the N.B.A. systematically escalated its efforts to scrub it from the game. The league did this because its leadership became more sensitive to fan and media outrage. In prior decades, sports were primarily covered locally, meaning that a particularly bad team in Cleveland which was obviously trying to lose would not necessarily catch the attention of a columnist at, say, the New York Post or the Los Angeles Times—and, in any case, those writers wouldn’t waste their column inches on the Cavaliers. During the 1996–97 season, for example, the Boston Celtics went 15–67 and effectively admitted to tanking for the right to draft Tim Duncan. (The effort was not successful.) This was a bit of a scandal at the time, but it didn’t lead the national sports news. Even now, not every mediocre team tries to lose every single game and maximize their draft odds—last year, the Sacramento Kings, who had one of the worst opening-day rosters in the league, tried to win games for much longer than reason would seem to dictate. But the media environment has changed. When all news is national and every outraged fan can post their thoughts on social media, a suspicious lineup in Utah in April can feed a daylong news cycle.

Under this interpretation of events, front offices aren’t necessarily more shameless than they were in the past; rather, shame itself is dictated by changes in the media and in technology. A competing theory might hold that, in the pre-Olajuwon era, a coin flip sufficed because the degrees of shame and basic decency were sufficient to prevent teams from doing what the Rockets did. Once the Rockets broke the shame seal and stole away with Olajuwon, the league needed to take drastic measures, because everyone would now feel emboldened to make a mockery of the game. This view suggests that the sense of shame was collectively weakened by a series of self-interested actors who shattered the social firmament and opened up the gates to chaos. The league’s anti-tanking rules are, then, responses to moral decline. Some amalgam of fan input, ticket sales, ratings, and media outrage determines what’s right and wrong, and this collective taste shifts more slowly than the behavior of front-office opportunists.

The McLuhanite in me wants to stick to the first interpretation, in which the apparent shift in shame is a matter of morality getting funnelled through a new medium. This kind of technological effect, detailed by Neil Postman in his book “Amusing Ourselves to Death,” provided the underlying premise of this column when it launched, and I still believe in its broad explanatory power. If it feels like all discourse has become unhinged and flooded with hate, full of provocations that once would have been shamed out of public life, this is probably because social media allows us the cover of anonymity and physical distance. Most people communicate digitally now, so most interactions are less mediated by shame. In person, you are much less likely to insult someone’s wife, for instance, because you would have to calculate the very real possibility that you would get punched in the face.

Sometimes, though, these genealogies of behavior can seem beside the point, serving only to dull one’s analysis of the situation. Twenty-four-hour news cycles, social media, and smartphones may have altered our sensitivity to shame, but they don’t explain everything. Social media has certainly helped spread what Foxworth called optimization culture, but the hiring of M.B.A.s and quants into management positions across markets didn’t happen because Elon Musk changed the Twitter algorithm. The kind of thinking that they embody has always been part of American capitalism—still, it’s everywhere now, and it’s worse.

In tech, finance, and, to a lesser degree, politics, those preaching a piecemeal gospel rooted in maximum optimization believe that they have obviated society’s need for shame. There is a conflict between those who still believe in social barriers and those who believe that all actions should be based on a proper calculation of the return on investment. That conflict constitutes both the present and the future of America’s culture war. The optimizers have all the money; the empaths only really have one another—and the assurance, however fleeting, that there are more of us than there are of them.

Efficient and sometimes monstrous thinking existed in the past, of course, but it generally made some effort to hide. Today, everything from our kids’ sports leagues to our parents’ nursing homes are profit-optimized right in front of our faces. Shame can no longer curtail a private-equity firm from buying up children’s sports facilities and shaving away every soft edge that made them feel like community property. Like the N.B.A., our world at large will need intervention and direct regulation to counter the gospel of flagrant optimization. ♦

title: It turns out 58% of The Blood of Dawnwalker players have also played The Witcher 3, and roughly 40% of the entire playerbase is on Steam
author: Sherif Saed
content:
The fangs showed up.

If you're familiar with the lineage of Rebel Wolves, the studio behind the recently-released The Blood of Dawnwalker, it may not surprise you to learn that a lot of the game's players are also fans of a certain other medieval fantasy RPG.

According to new data by industry analysts at Alinea Analytics, nearly 58 percent of Dawnwalker players have also played The Witcher 3. Rebel Wolves, of course, is a team made up of many former Witcher developers and CD Projekt Red alumni. The games share a few other similarities, too, such as being centred around a protagonist with superpowers they didn't ask for in a world that doesn't always like or appreciate them.

Analyst Rhys Elliott also revealed in the same report that Poland is the game's second-largest market on Steam, with 11 percent of players. The US is far ahead at number one, though, with 34 percent. It's clear local players showed up, given that both Rebel Wolves and CDPR are Polish studios.

Speaking of shared audiences, The Blood of Dawnwalker's players cross-over with a number of other recent releases in the same or similar genres. According to the report, 13 percent of players have played Mortal Shell 2, and 9 percent have played Onimusha: Way of the Sword.

Rebel Wolves recently announced Dawnwalker has sold over one million copies in its first three days on sale. Alinea estimates 410,000 of those sales were made on Steam, noting it "also did well" on GOG, the DRM-free PC game store. Given how large the game's PC audience appears to be, Dawnwalker has a growing mod scene, though the most popular mod so far removes its main time mechanic.

In the Eurogamer review of The Blood of Dawnwalker, Bertie was happy with how the game used said time mechanic to create meaningful stakes, even if that brilliance doesn't always come across elsewhere in the game.

title: Here are our PS Plus Premium and Extra games for September
author: Robert Purchese
content:
Slitterhead! Ball x Pit! Ninja Gaiden!

Sony has revealed the games coming to PlayStation Plus Premium and Extra in September and there's some decent stuff, although it lacks a glitzy headliner like, say, Big Walk last month.

Here's the September PS Plus Extra and Premium list:

  • Date Everything! - 9th September (PS5)
  • RuneScape: Dragonwilds - 15th September (PS5)
  • WWE 2K26 - 15th September (PS5)
  • Slitterhead - 22nd September (PS4, PS5)
  • Ball x Pit (PS5) - 22nd September
  • Ninja Gaiden: Ragebound - 29th September (PS4, PS5)
  • Dungeons of Hinterberg - 29th September (PS4, PS5)
  • Sniper Elite: Resistance - 29th September (PS4, PS5)

And just for PS Premium:

  • Mega Man X Command Mission - 15th September (PS4, PS5)
  • Metro Redux - 15th September (PS4)

The highlight in September, as with Xbox Game Pass this month, is the arrival of third-person RuneScape co-op survival game Dragonwilds. I think it looks good and it has a solid reputation on Steam, where it's been in early access for a year or so. Dragonwilds arrives next week, on Tuesday 15th September.

Besides Dragonwilds, it's mostly slightly older games from a year or two ago arriving on PS Plus, though there are some bangers among them. There's Ball x Pit, which is a fiendishly compelling roguelike take on Breakout - I lost hours to it, quite happily. There's the raunchy and often hilarious dating game Date Everything, where you chat up personified furniture around your house, and there's the bizarre but well-reviewed action horror game Slitterhead from a couple of years ago.

There's the imaginative anime modern world fantasy RPG Dungeons of Hinterberg, which also reviewed well a couple of years back; there's Sniper Elite Resistance, which again reviewed well relatively recently; and there's the widely acclaimed retro-styled, side-scroller Ninja Gaiden Ragebound from last year, which we didn't review but I've heard great things about. And, of course, if you're a fan of things Metro or Mega Man, this month's Premium offerings are for you.
